UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Decision - 20 COM VIII.A 

 Inscription: Lake Baikal (Russian Federation) 

Lake Baikal

754

Russian Federation 

N(i) (ii) (iii) (iv) 

The Committee inscribed Lake Baikal as the most outstanding example of a freshwater ecosystem on the basis of natural criteria (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). It is the oldest and deepest of the world's lakes containing nearly 20% of the world's unfrozen freshwater reserve. The lake contains an outstanding variety of endemic flora and fauna, which is of exceptional value to evolutionary science. It is also surrounded by a system of protected areas that have high scenic and other natural values. The Committee took note of the confirmation of the revised boundaries of the site, which correspond to the core areas defined in the Baikal Law (excluding the five urban developed areas). It also noted that the special Lake Baikal Law is now in its second reading in the Duma. Finally, it noted concern over a number of integrity issues including pollution, which should be brought to the attention of the Russian authorities.

evidence.title: Deepest lake | Guinness World Records
evidence.excerpt:
# Deepest lake

Who

Lake Baikal

What

 1,642 metre(s) 

Where

 Russian Federation 

When

 1999 

Lake Baikal is a freshwater lake located in a geological rift valley in south-eastern Siberia. Soundings taken from the lake's Central Basin revealed it to be 1,642 metres (5,387 feet) deep. The lake is 636 kilometres (395 miles) long, with an average width of only 48 kilometres (30 miles). A volume of 23,615.390 cubic kilometres (5,665.63 cubic miles) also makes it the largest freshwater lake by volume.

The lake has an area of 31,722 square kilometres (12,247 square miles).

Baikal's depth and volume is based on the findings of a bottom-relief survey carried out by Navy Hydrographic Survey expeditions in 1979–87, which were compiled into bathymetric maps in 1992. This data was digitized, corrected and updated with material from other surveys in 1999. Funding for the project was provided by INTAS (International Association for the promotion of cooperation with scientists from the New Independent States of the former Soviet Union).

The revised depth and volume of Lake Baikal were published in the report "Computer-based Bathymetric Map of Lake Baikal", which appeared in Doklady Earth Sciences, vol. 408, issue 1, in May 2006. The authors of the report are P P Sherstyankin, S P Alekseev, A M Abramov, K G Stavrov, M De Batist, R His, M Canals and J L Casamor.

evidence.excerpt:

## Don't confuse with

- Caspian Sea: the largest inland water body by area (about 371,000 sq km). But it is saltwater and sits in a closed basin. Baikal is the deepest and oldest, and its water is fresh.
- Lake Superior: the largest freshwater lake by area (about 82,100 sq km) [3]. Baikal is the deepest lake, not the largest by area.
- Lake Tanganyika: the longest freshwater lake (about 670 km) and the second deepest (about 1,470 m). Baikal is first in depth.
- Lake Victoria: Africa's largest lake. It sits on a plateau between the two arms of the East African Rift, so it is not a rift lake. Baikal, Tanganyika and Malawi are rift lakes.

...

- Deepest and oldest lake in the world: Baikal (about 1,700 m per UNESCO; about 1,642 m per NCERT; about 25 million years old) [1].
- Depth order, deepest first: Baikal > Tanganyika > Malawi.
- Type: Baikal is a rift lake, like Tanganyika and Malawi. Trap: Lake Victoria is not a rift lake.
- Lake Baikal became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 and holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen fresh water [1].
- Nerpa (Baikal seal): one of the few seals that live only in fresh water. Baikal is called the "Galapagos of Russia" [1].
- Endemic count: about 745 of 1,340 animal species and 150 of 570 plant species are endemic [1].

# Deepest lake

Who

Lake Baikal

What

 1,642 metre(s) 

Where

 Russian Federation 

When

 1999 

Lake Baikal is a freshwater lake located in a geological rift valley in south-eastern Siberia. Soundings taken from the lake's Central Basin revealed it to be 1,642 metres (5,387 feet) deep. The lake is 636 kilometres (395 miles) long, with an average width of only 48 kilometres (30 miles). A volume of 23,615.390 cubic kilometres (5,665.63 cubic miles) also makes it the largest freshwater lake by volume.

The lake has an area of 31,722 square kilometres (12,247 square miles).

Baikal's depth and volume is based on the findings of a bottom-relief survey carried out by Navy Hydrographic Survey expeditions in 1979–87, which were compiled into bathymetric maps in 1992. This data was digitized, corrected and updated with material from other surveys in 1999. Funding for the project was provided by INTAS (International Association for the promotion of cooperation with scientists from the New Independent States of the former Soviet Union).

The revised depth and volume of Lake Baikal were published in the report "Computer-based Bathymetric Map of Lake Baikal", which appeared in Doklady Earth Sciences, vol. 408, issue 1, in May 2006. The authors of the report are P P Sherstyankin, S P Alekseev, A M Abramov, K G Stavrov, M De Batist, R His, M Canals and J L Casamor.
